findings.quote: The default cap pins layers 0 to 15 (address order, first fit), which carry
findings.problem: This is wrong about what gets pinned, and so about where the 49% comes from. pin_host_experts does first fit over individual tensors, not whole layers. The RAM/4 cap (31.11 GiB / 4 = 7964 MiB) fits layers 0 to 15 (7522 MiB) plus layer 16's down and gate tensors (176 + 144 MiB = 7842 MiB). Only layer 16's up tensor is left out. The 49% is the share of that whole pinned set. Layers 0 to 15 alone carry 47.8%. The same wording, newly written, appears in ROADMAP.md ("default 7842 MiB pins layers 0 to 15 and covers about 49% of the warm upload bytes") and in STATE.md step 2 ("The default pins layers 0 to 15 (address order, first fit), about 49% of the warm upload bytes").
findings.evidence: Read the GGUF header (pure-Python parser, read only). Expert tensors are separate ranges with 1 to 38 MiB gaps between them, so none merge. Per layer: 464 MiB, except layer 1 at 562 MiB and layers 34, 38 and 39 at 498 MiB. Cumulative size through layer 15 is 7522 MiB; adding blk.16 down (176) and gate (144) gives 7842, which matches log_2048-pinned_long.txt "registered 7842.20 MiB". The trace agrees: in C:/nsys/exp0004/2048-pinned_long.sqlite, tokens 387-1022, layer 16's copies are 576 KiB pinned x1673, 704 KiB pinned x1673 and 576 KiB pageable x1673, so 69% of its bytes are pinned. Layers 0-15 are 47.84% of expert upload bytes and the whole pinned set is 49.33%. The same per-tensor rule explains the 15266 MiB cap exactly: 14946 (layers 0-31) + 176 + 144 = 15266. So layer 32's up tensor stays pageable as well, about 0.8% more traffic. Layers 33-39 alone are 17.5%.
findings.fix: The default cap pins layers 0 to 15 and the gate and down tensors of layer 16 (address order, first fit per tensor), which carry about 49% of the warm upload bytes (layers 0 to 15 alone 48%) for 42% of the expert bytes, ... Make the same change in ROADMAP.md R11 and STATE.md step 2. Optionally add that at 15266 MiB the same rule leaves layer 32's up tensor and layers 33 to 39 pageable, about 18% of the warm upload bytes.

findings.quote: pages in. Yet no pinned copy ever waited on a fault (0 slow pinned copies in
findings.problem: The number is wrong. One pinned expert copy is slow, in 2048-pinned_t2. The fix behind this text (doc_check finding 3) checked only three of the five pinned captures. The review had already said one pinned copy was slow. Sign 4 repeats the claim: "No pinned copy ever waited on a fault." (line 242).
findings.evidence: timeline_2048-pinned_t2.json summary.expert_copy_rates has "pinned/slow": n = 1, next to "pinned/fast": n = 20151. A read-only query of C:/nsys/exp0004/2048-pinned_t2.sqlite finds it: a 589,824 B pinned copy whose host call took 5169 us (0.11 GB/s), in decode token 66, which is inside the analysed window. The other four pinned captures have 0 below 1.5 GB/s. Across all five captures that is 1 slow copy out of 296,533 pinned expert copies. review.json pagefault C4: "only 1 of ~250k was slow". The trace cannot say whether this one copy waited on a fault.
findings.fix: Yet only 1 of about 296,500 pinned expert copies in the five pinned captures was slow (576 KiB in 5.2 ms, 2048 MiB pinned rep 2, decode token 66; prefill included); when those pages become resident is not measured. In sign 4, replace "No pinned copy ever waited on a fault." with "Only 1 of about 296,500 pinned copies was slow."

findings.quote: overlap ceiling; the wider literature reports 5 to 34% (SOURCES.md).
findings.problem: The sentence mixes two units. The "8 to 15%" just before it is a share of token time. The 5 to 34% is Eliseev-Mazur's gain in tokens per second (ratios of their Table 2). As a share of token time, +34% is about 25%. ROADMAP.md R13 has the same mix: "the two closest studies measure 8 to 15% of token time from prefetch alone, the wider literature 5 to 34% (SOURCES.md)".
findings.evidence: SOURCES.md, Eliseev and Mazur row: "+5% A100, +11% RTX 3060, +19% RTX 3080 Mobile, +34% T4 (ratios of their Table 2)". literature.json gives the tokens/s figures: T4 2.092 against 1.567 = 1.335x, so 1 - 1/1.335 = 25% of token time. The other wide-literature gains are also speedups: AdapMoE 1.22x (18% of time), Fate about +30% (about 23%).
findings.fix: ...overlap ceiling; the wider literature reports +5 to +34% tokens per second (about 5 to 25% of token time) (SOURCES.md). Make the same change in ROADMAP.md R13: "the wider literature +5 to +34% tokens per second (5 to 25% of token time)".

findings.quote: - **Record the prefill time** as a coldness check: 13.4 to 13.8 s cold for the
findings.problem: The cold reference covers only pageable runs. A cold run with 42% pinned prefills in 9.3 to 9.9 s and makes about 3600 prefill slow copies, not 6480. Under this check a cold pinned arm would look partly warm. STATE.md step 1 says the same ("coldness check (cold is 13.4 to 13.8 s and about 6480)"), and its step 3 runs pinned arms at 7842 and 15000 MiB. ROADMAP.md R10 also says "prefill slow copies (about 6480 when cold)".
findings.evidence: Prompt eval times in log_*pinned*.txt: 1024 pinned t1/t2/u 9325 / 9332 / 9360 ms; 2048 pinned t1/t2/u/long 9767 / 9755 / 9946 / 9523 ms. All of these runs were cold: review.json synthesis says "Pinned runs start the same whatever ran before (32.80 vs 32.84 slow/token)". Read-only count of prefill expert copies below 1.5 GB/s (before the first logits read-back): 3638 (2048-pinned_t1), 3708 (1024-pinned_t1), 3574 (2048-pinned_long), against 6484 (2048-pageable_t1).
findings.fix: - **Record the prefill time** as a coldness check: cold is 13.4 to 13.8 s for the 46-token prompt with pageable experts and 9.3 to 9.9 s with 42% pinned; 3.7 to 7.3 s means an earlier run left the model partly cached. In STATE.md step 1, write "(cold pageable is 13.4 to 13.8 s and about 6480; cold with 42% pinned 9.3 to 9.9 s and about 3600; record a cold reference for each pinned size)", and qualify ROADMAP.md R10's "about 6480 when cold" as pageable.

findings.quote: - Tokens 1 and 2 include graph capture and are excluded; every 256th token
findings.problem: This is the error doc_check finding 8 fixed in EXP-0004.md, surviving here. Token 1 does no graph capture; it runs eagerly. Only token 2 captures. Capture also is not why the two tokens are slow: most of their time is page-fault idle.
findings.evidence: Read-only API counts in C:/nsys/exp0004/2048-pageable_t1.sqlite. Token 1 (448.9 ms): 1646 cudaLaunchKernel, with no cudaStreamBeginCapture and no cudaGraphLaunch. Token 2 (692.6 ms): 41 cudaStreamBeginCapture / EndCapture / GraphInstantiate plus 41 cudaGraphLaunch. Token 3: 41 cudaGraphLaunch only. doc_check finding 8 gives slow-copy idle of 320.1 and 604.8 ms in those two tokens. EXP-0004.md now reads "token 1 runs eagerly and token 2 captures the graphs, but most of their time is page-fault idle".
findings.fix: - Tokens 1 and 2 are excluded (token 1 runs eagerly, token 2 captures the graphs, and both are mostly page-fault idle); every 256th token re-captures and runs most graphs eagerly.

findings.quote: order is already a fair miss-frequency order at layer granularity; what is left
findings.problem: The data do not support this at the WDDM cap. The layers that address order leaves pageable there (33 to 39) are average, not the least missed: 17.5% of warm traffic for 17.9% of expert bytes. Choosing the pageable layers by miss frequency, with no expert-level work, would leave about 13 to 14% of traffic pageable instead of about 18%. So a gain remains at layer granularity, not only within layers.
findings.evidence: Per-layer expert upload bytes from C:/nsys/exp0004/2048-pageable_long.sqlite, tokens 387-1022 (633 tokens with 41 graphs, read only). Layers 33-39 carry 17.48%; with layer 32's up tensor, which first fit also leaves pageable, 18.3%. The 3494 MiB left pageable at 15266 MiB, filled with the layers lowest in traffic per MiB (14, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 26, 35), carries 14.0% while using 3712 MiB; at exactly 3494 MiB it is about 13.5%. Layer sizes come from the GGUF header.
findings.fix: So address order roughly tracks miss frequency in the lowest layers, but not at the tail: at the cap, choosing the pageable layers by miss frequency would leave about 13 to 14% of warm traffic pageable instead of about 18%, and ordering experts within layers can add to that. Both need per-(layer, expert) miss counts from EXP-0001's traces through the simulator.

findings.quote: | overlap upload with compute, perfect next-layer prediction | **-9.4 ms** (17%); -10.4 with unlimited lookahead | copy stream plus prediction; at 70-90% recall still 8.8 to 9.1 |
findings.problem: The table mixes windows. Finding 10 declares its base as tokens 387 to 1022, and -9.4 is on that base. findings.fix: KNOWLEDGE_BASE.md: "at 70-90% recall still 8.9 to 9.2" (or keep 8.8 to 9.1 and add "on tokens 771 to 898"). In OPEN_QUESTIONS.md Q7: "and 70 to 90% recall still 8.9 to 9.2 ms".

findings.quote: `cudaMemcpyAsync` from pageable memory is neither asynchronous nor full speed: it
findings.problem: This sentence was written before EXP-0004, and it continues "goes through a driver staging buffer". It blames the staging buffer for the slow pageable copies. EXP-0004 found that a pageable DMA runs at full speed unless the host is staging the next copy at the same time. KNOWLEDGE_BASE.md Finding 4 now says the opposite of this sentence.
findings.evidence: KNOWLEDGE_BASE.md Finding 4: pageable copies run at 12.9 to 13.1 GB/s when the host is not staging the next copy, against 12.8 GB/s pinned. It also says "a pageable copy is not slow because of the staging copy as such but because the host's staging of the next copy slows the current DMA by about 37%". EXP-0004.md "DMA rates" gives 8.2 GB/s contended against 12.9 to 13.1 GB/s uncontended. The memory pathway diagram in this file ("pageable 13 GB/s alone, 8.2 contended") agrees with EXP-0004, so this sentence contradicts its own file.
findings.fix: `cudaMemcpyAsync` from pageable memory is not asynchronous: it goes through a driver staging buffer and blocks the host. Its DMA runs at full speed (12.9 to 13.1 GB/s) unless the host is staging the next pageable copy at the same time, when it drops to 8.2 GB/s (EXP-0004; KNOWLEDGE_BASE.md Finding 4).
